title: Founder departure can disrupt startup retention after workers build shared relationships and culture
source_unit: Census CES Working Paper CES-26-21; matched U.S. employer-employee data with founder premature-death cases used as plausibly exogenous founder exits
geography: United States startups and their employees; matched Census employer-employee records

observations.period: U.S. startup founder departure and employee retention; matched administrative study, paper published March 2026

denominator.unit: study-defined matched startup and employee analysis

founder_departure.value: founder departures significantly increased employee turnover

firm_age_size.value: the turnover effect was stronger in older and larger startups
firm_age_size.unit: heterogeneous effect by startup age and size

shared_tenure.value: the departure effect was more salient among employees with longer shared tenure with the founder

same_sex.value: the departure effect was more salient among employees who had the same sex as the founder

proposed_mechanism.value: the patterns suggest complementarities in skills, relationships, or culture develop between founders and employees over time

observations.method: The paper uses matched employer-employee Census data and focuses on premature founder deaths as plausibly exogenous exits to study employee turnover after founder departure. It compares effects by startup age, size, shared tenure, and employee-founder sex.
observations.uncertainty: The source measures turnover, not whether leaving was voluntary, beneficial, harmful, or caused by worsening conditions. Founder death is an unusual departure and may differ from resignation, acquisition, conflict, or planned succession. The abstract does not observe pay, job quality, worker voice, replacement leadership, firm survival, household effects, or later careers.
observations.subgroup: Employees and startups in the matched U.S. Census analysis; effects may differ by occupation, founder role, ownership, industry, worker identity, firm governance, local labor market, and type of founder departure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher turnover after founder death may reflect grief, uncertainty, leadership replacement, firm strategy, financing, or other disruption rather than a positive founder-employee cultural bond. Longer tenure or same-sex matching may proxy role, hierarchy, occupation, or selection rather than shared culture.

related_sources.claim: Official Census PDF for CES Working Paper CES-26-21

boundary: This record adds a founder-culture and retention mechanism: a firm can depend on relationships, skills, and meaning built around a person. It does not establish that founder influence is good or bad, that turnover reflects worker harm, or that founder departure changes firm survival, worker control, household security, or broader culture.
